# Digest R0 — Prefaces + Introduction (Moo James PNTC)
**Range:** cache R0 (raw L135–155 + L275–523; biblio L161–269 excluded)
**Agent coverage:** Full cache file read (~274 lines / ~19,882 words): D. A. Carson series note; Moo author’s preface; Introduction from reception/popularity through genre, authorship (traditional case + four objections + pseudepigraphy + brother-of-Lord views), occasion/readers, date, theology (God, eschatology, law, wisdom, poverty/wealth, Christian life, faith/works/justification + covenantal nomism), structure and central concern (spiritual wholeness). No commentary on specific pericope blocks beyond introductory survey.

## Claims

### C-R0-001
- **Claim:** Pillar NT commentaries aim at clear exposition of the biblical text for serious pastors and teachers, blending rigorous exegesis with exposition and biblical theology while avoiding undue technical detail and not confusing commentary with sermon.
- **Attribution:** D. A. Carson (series preface)
- **Quote:** "Designed for serious pastors and teachers of the Bible, the Pillar commentaries seek above all to make clear the text of Scripture as we have it."
- **Locus:** Series preface (Carson), opening paragraph
- **Tags:** [moo-james-pntc, douglas-moo]
- **Type:** structure

### C-R0-002
- **Claim:** Carson rejects “objective scholarship” as a vain chimera that may be profane; series writers aim for evenhanded openness to the text as the best kind of objectivity, with reverence and questing obedience because the text is God’s Word.
- **Attribution:** D. A. Carson
- **Quote:** "the vision of \"objective scholarship\" (a vain chimera) may actually be profane. God stands over against us; we do not stand in judgment of him."
- **Locus:** Series preface (Carson)
- **Tags:** [moo-james-pntc]
- **Type:** position

### C-R0-003
- **Claim:** Carson presents Moo’s James volume as more than an enlargement of Moo’s TNTC James; it is a fresh, detailed work with deceptive simplicity of style and a gentle tone of thoughtful pastoral application.
- **Attribution:** D. A. Carson
- **Quote:** "More than an enlargement of his well-received little commentary on James in the TNTC series, this volume is a fresh and detailed work"
- **Locus:** Series preface, Carson’s commendation of Moo
- **Tags:** [moo-james-pntc, douglas-moo, james]
- **Type:** reception

### C-R0-004
- **Claim:** Moo’s PNTC James revisits his 1985 Tyndale (TNTC) commentary about fifteen years later, nearly doubling the space for background and theology; he is more impressed by James’s creative use of Hellenistic Jewish traditions and remains convinced the letter’s heart is a call to wholehearted commitment to Christ.
- **Attribution:** Moo
- **Quote:** "fifteen years ago I wrote a commentary on James for the Tyndale series… The Pillar series has enabled me almost to double the space… I remain convinced that the heart of the letter is a call to wholehearted commitment to Christ."
- **Locus:** Author’s preface (Moo)
- **Tags:** [moo-james-pntc, douglas-moo, james]
- **Type:** fact

### C-R0-005
- **Claim:** Moo dedicates the book to his wife Jenny and thanks Carson, Milton Essenburg, Stephen Pegler, Leigh Swain, and Pierce Yates for editorial/research help.
- **Attribution:** Moo
- **Quote:** "most of all I want to thank my wife Jenny, to whom I dedicate this book."
- **Locus:** Author’s preface
- **Tags:** [moo-james-pntc, douglas-moo]
- **Type:** fact

### C-R0-006
- **Claim:** James has been highly controversial: its canonical place was contested by some early Christians; Luther called it an “epistle of straw”; modern theologians often dismiss it as a Jewish holdover—yet among ordinary believers it is among the two or three most popular NT books.
- **Attribution:** Moo
- **Quote:** "The reformer Martin Luther called it an \"epistle of straw\" and relegated it to a secondary status within the NT."
- **Locus:** Intro opening (reception / popularity)
- **Tags:** [james, douglas-moo]
- **Type:** reception

### C-R0-007
- **Claim:** Moo explains James’s popular appeal by three traits: intense practicality (highest frequency of imperative verbs in the NT; purpose to chastise, exhort, encourage more than inform); conciseness and rapid movement among topics (somewhat like Proverbs); lavish metaphors/illustrations of universal appeal.
- **Attribution:** Moo
- **Quote:** "the Letter of James contains a higher frequency of imperative verbs than any other NT book."
- **Locus:** Intro, three characteristics of popularity
- **Tags:** [james, douglas-moo, wisdom-literature]
- **Type:** position

### C-R0-008
- **Claim:** Early Christians classed James with 1–2 Peter, 1–3 John, and Jude as a “general” or “catholic” letter because of its general address (“the twelve tribes scattered among the nations,” 1:1); James was not finally recognized by both eastern and western church until the fourth century.
- **Attribution:** Moo
- **Quote:** "James was not finally recognized by both the eastern and western parts of the church until the fourth century."
- **Locus:** Intro, early reception / canon history
- **Tags:** [james, douglas-moo]
- **Type:** fact

### C-R0-009
- **Claim:** On early use, Moo follows L. T. Johnson over Mayor’s maximal allusions: a good case can be made that 1 Clement (Rome c. A.D. 95) and The Shepherd of Hermas depend on James; similarities with Hermas’s Mandates are particularly striking.
- **Attribution:** Moo citing L. T. Johnson (vs. J. B. Mayor)
- **Quote:** "He thinks a good case can be made that two Christian books from the late first and early second century depend on James: 1 Clement… and The Shepherd of Hermas"
- **Locus:** Intro, early reception
- **Tags:** [james, douglas-moo]
- **Type:** position

### C-R0-010
- **Claim:** Origen is the first to cite James by name, attributing it to James “the apostle” and citing it as Scripture; in Latin translations the author is more explicitly “brother of the Lord,” but reliability of that addition is doubted.
- **Attribution:** Moo (on Origen)
- **Quote:** "Origen, is the first to cite James by name. He attributes the letter to James, \"the apostle\" (Commentary on John, frag. 126), and cites the letter as Scripture"
- **Locus:** Intro, early reception
- **Tags:** [james, douglas-moo, james-the-just]
- **Type:** fact

### C-R0-011
- **Claim:** Eusebius cites James as canonical yet relegates it to the “disputed books” (antilegomena) category (Hist. Eccl. 3.25.3; 2.23.25); doubts often came from the Syrian church (e.g. Theodore of Mopsuestia rejected general letters), though James entered the fifth-century Syriac NT and was approved by Chrysostom and Theodoret.
- **Attribution:** Moo (on Eusebius and Syriac reception)
- **Quote:** "he also relegates it to the status of a \"disputed book\" in his survey of the state of the canon in his day (History of the Church 3.25.3; 2.23.25)."
- **Locus:** Intro, early reception
- **Tags:** [james, douglas-moo]
- **Type:** reception

### C-R0-012
- **Claim:** In the West, neither the Muratorian Canon nor the Mommsen catalog includes James; earliest undisputed western reference is mid-fourth century (Hilary, Ambrosiaster); Jerome’s Vulgate endorsement and frequent citation (author as brother of the Lord), followed by Augustine, secured James’s place.
- **Attribution:** Moo
- **Quote:** "Decisive, perhaps, for James's eventual place in the canon of the western church was the endorsement of the major figure Jerome."
- **Locus:** Intro, western reception
- **Tags:** [james, douglas-moo, james-the-just]
- **Type:** reception

### C-R0-013
- **Claim:** Moo argues slow/hesitant adoption does not warrant modern doubt about authenticity or authority: James was neglected more than rejected; neglect explained by preference for apostolic books, common name “James,” practical rather than theological profile, misuse by Jewish-Christian groups, and destination to Palestinian/Syrian churches disrupted by the 66–70 and 132–35 revolts.
- **Attribution:** Moo
- **Quote:** "the evidence we possess suggests that James was not so much rejected as neglected."
- **Locus:** Intro, evaluation of slow canonization
- **Tags:** [james, douglas-moo, james-authorship]
- **Type:** position

### C-R0-014
- **Claim:** At the Reformation, Erasmus doubted apostolic origin on grounds of good Greek; Luther’s objections were primarily theological—justification by faith as the doctrine on which the church stands or falls—leading him to say James “mangles the Scriptures and thereby opposes Paul” and to call it an “epistle of straw,” relegated with Jude, Hebrews, and Revelation to the end of the NT; yet Luther did not exclude James and still quoted it.
- **Attribution:** Moo on Luther (and Erasmus)
- **Quote:** "Hence Luther claimed that James \"mangles the Scriptures and thereby opposes Paul and all Scripture\" (LW 35:397). James was \"an epistle of straw\" (LW 35:362)"
- **Locus:** Intro, Reformation reception
- **Tags:** [james, douglas-moo, james-paul-justification, justification]
- **Type:** reception

### C-R0-015
- **Claim:** Moo endorses Calvin’s approach against Luther’s: Calvin accepted full apostolic authority, noted James seems sparing on grace yet not all apostles must treat the same arguments, and held Paul and James on justification can be harmonized; with Jewish background better appreciated, James is a needed counterweight to imbalance from reading Paul alone.
- **Attribution:** Moo (following Calvin’s approach)
- **Quote:** "Calvin, for instance, while admitting that James \"seems more sparing in proclaiming the grace of Christ than it behooved an Apostle to be,\" also rightly noted that \"it is not surely required for all to handle the same arguments.\""
- **Locus:** Intro, Reformation / post-Calvin standard reception
- **Tags:** [james, douglas-moo, james-paul-justification, justification]
- **Type:** position

### C-R0-016
- **Claim:** Formally a letter (1:1) but lacking typical personal greetings, co-workers, travel plans, and specific named situations (situations often vague/hypothetical: 2:2–3, 15–17; 4:13–17), James is more a “literary” than personal letter; closest NT parallel perhaps 1 John; early “general letter” classification overstates universality—most scholars agree it addresses a specific church or group of churches.
- **Attribution:** Moo
- **Quote:** "James is therefore more a \"literary\" than a personal letter; the closest parallel to it in the NT is perhaps 1 John."
- **Locus:** Intro, Nature/Genre
- **Tags:** [james, douglas-moo]
- **Type:** position

### C-R0-017
- **Claim:** James depends more than any other NT author on Jesus’ teaching (often via Matthean forms; 5:12 nearly quotes Matt. 5:33–37 on oaths) and shows striking similarities to Hellenistic Judaism (Philo, Sirach, Testaments of the Twelve Patriarchs); the author seems “soaked” in Jesus’ teaching.
- **Attribution:** Moo
- **Quote:** "James depends more than any other NT author on the teaching of Jesus."
- **Locus:** Intro, Nature/Genre (traditional sources)
- **Tags:** [james, douglas-moo, wisdom-literature]
- **Type:** position

### C-R0-018
- **Claim:** Dibelius classified James as *paraenesis* (exhortation; general situation; traditional material; loose organization); Moo reports this once-influential view has waned—scholars doubt paraenesis as an ancient identifiable genre and now find binding motifs/themes where Dibelius saw isolated sayings.
- **Attribution:** Moo on Dibelius and recent scholarship
- **Quote:** "These three facets of the letter, combined with its hortatory focus, led Martin Dibelius to classify the letter as paraenesis."
- **Locus:** Intro, Nature/Genre
- **Tags:** [james, douglas-moo]
- **Type:** position

### C-R0-019
- **Claim:** Wisdom is now the most popular genre identification (3:13–18; 1:5; proverb-like style; speech, wealth, dissension themes), but Moo rejects categorizing James as a whole as wisdom except under an unjustifiably broad definition—wisdom is not central and most of the letter is not proverb material.
- **Attribution:** Moo
- **Quote:** "only a very broad definition of \"wisdom\" would enable us to categorize James as a whole as wisdom; and we are not convinced that so broad a definition is justified."
- **Locus:** Intro, Nature/Genre
- **Tags:** [james, douglas-moo, wisdom-literature]
- **Type:** position

### C-R0-020
- **Claim:** Moo’s preferred specific label: James is best thought of as a sermon or homily put in letter form by an author separated from his readers by distance.
- **Attribution:** Moo
- **Quote:** "Perhaps the closest we can get to anything specific is to think of James as a sermon or homily."
- **Locus:** Intro, Nature/Genre (closing preference)
- **Tags:** [james, douglas-moo]
- **Type:** position

### C-R0-021
- **Claim:** Of NT Jameses, only James the brother of the Lord fits as author without further self-identification: James son of Zebedee died under Herod Agrippa I (Acts 12:2, ~A.D. 44)—too early for the letter; James son of Alphaeus is too obscure; James father of Judas is barely known; with few late exceptions, tradition identifies the Lord’s brother.
- **Attribution:** Moo
- **Quote:** "with a few late exceptions, Christians have traditionally identified the author of the letter with James the brother of the Lord."
- **Locus:** Intro § Author
- **Tags:** [james, douglas-moo, james-the-just, james-authorship]
- **Type:** position

### C-R0-022
- **Claim:** Corroborating points for James of Jerusalem: verbal similarities between the letter and James’s Acts 15 speech/letter (chairein greeting; “name” + passive kaleō; “listen, my brothers”); readers as Jewish Christians in economic distress under wealthy landowners fits mid-first-century Middle East and Acts 11:19 scatter after Stephen; primitive Christian theology (Jesus as Lord and coming judge; already/not-yet; elders) fits early Jewish-Christian environment.
- **Attribution:** Moo
- **Quote:** "the situation Luke describes in Acts 11:19 fits very neatly with the scenario we are proposing"
- **Locus:** Intro § Author (corroborating circumstances)
- **Tags:** [james, douglas-moo, james-the-just, james-authorship]
- **Type:** position

### C-R0-023
- **Claim:** Authorship matters for historical/canonical context (e.g. chap. 2 on justification) and for truthfulness: if not a James but someone writing in the famous brother’s name, either deception (false apostolic authority) or a literary device of reapplication is at issue—either affects attributed authority.
- **Attribution:** Moo
- **Quote:** "if… the person who wrote the letter was not a person named James but someone writing in the name of the famous brother of the Lord, then new questions arise."
- **Locus:** Intro § Author (why authorship debate matters)
- **Tags:** [james-authorship, douglas-moo, james]
- **Type:** position

### C-R0-024
- **Claim:** Moo quickly rejects (1) the curiosity that James is a lightly Christianized Jewish document (1:1; 2:1)—defeated by pervasive Jesus-teaching, and (2) authorship by James son of Alphaeus (Calvin) or an unknown James (Erasmus, Luther)—none of the strengths and all of the weaknesses of the traditional identification.
- **Attribution:** Moo
- **Quote:** "the decisive blow to this extreme view is the degree to which the letter is permeated with references to the teaching of Jesus."
- **Locus:** Intro § Author (alternative theories briefly)
- **Tags:** [james-authorship, douglas-moo, james]
- **Type:** position

### C-R0-025
- **Claim:** Dominant modern alternative: unknown Christian author; “James” in 1:1 added later (originally anonymous) or by the author (pseudepigraphy to lend authority / link teaching to the Lord’s brother). Moo examines four standard objections to authorship by the Lord’s brother.
- **Attribution:** Moo (reporting critical consensus)
- **Quote:** "This latter theory now dominates modern scholarship on James."
- **Locus:** Intro § Author (critical alternative)
- **Tags:** [james-authorship, douglas-moo, james-the-just]
- **Type:** position

### C-R0-026
- **Claim:** Objection 1: a brother of Jesus would have mentioned the relationship and/or the resurrection appearance (1 Cor. 15:7). Moo: argument from silence; physical tie not basis of James’s authority in Acts; estrangement during Jesus’ ministry; failure to mention relation actually weighs *against* pseudepigraphy; Tasker notes capriciousness (James vs. 2 Peter); occasional letters make such arguments tenuous.
- **Attribution:** Moo (replying to critical objection)
- **Quote:** "If anything, therefore, the author's failure to mention the relationship is an argument against the pseudepigraphical view."
- **Locus:** Intro § Author, objection 1
- **Tags:** [james-authorship, douglas-moo, james-the-just]
- **Type:** position

### C-R0-027
- **Claim:** Objection 2: quality of Greek (higher koine; incomplete hexameter 1:17) and Hellenistic cultural allusions (Sirach, Testaments, Philo; “cycle of nature” 3:6) exceed a Galilean carpenter’s son who never left Palestine. Moo: Greek is not literary (Ropes); philosophical terms had entered mainstream language; Hengel on Hellenistic penetration of Palestine; many Galileans fluent in Greek; Sevenster concludes James of Jerusalem *could* have written it—Greek is no obstacle (not proof of authorship).
- **Attribution:** Moo (citing Ropes, Hengel, Sevenster)
- **Quote:** "J. N. Sevenster… concludes that James of Jerusalem could have written this letter… the Greek of the letter constitutes no obstacle to the ascription of the letter to James."
- **Locus:** Intro § Author, objection 2
- **Tags:** [james-authorship, douglas-moo, james-the-just]
- **Type:** position

### C-R0-028
- **Claim:** Objection 3: letter’s “liberal” ethical focus (“law of liberty,” “royal law”; silence on ritual law) conflicts with NT and tradition picturing James enforcing kosher (Gal. 2:11–13), temple rites (Acts 21:20–25), and “torah-piety.” Moo: Hegesippus/Josephus confirm death by stoning A.D. 62, but radical Jewish-Christian “capture” of James is tendentious legend; NT James was loyal to torah for Jewish Christians/evangelism without requiring that he always write about ritual law; silence is occasional, not anti-ritual; Jesus too stressed ethics without dismissing ritual (Matt. 23:23).
- **Attribution:** Moo
- **Quote:** "the picture of James as \"an advocate of hidebound Jewish-Christian piety\" is a legend with no basis in fact."
- **Locus:** Intro § Author, objection 3
- **Tags:** [james-authorship, douglas-moo, james-the-just]
- **Type:** position

### C-R0-029
- **Claim:** Objection 4 (James–Paul justification): James 2:24 requires works for justification vs. Paul (Rom. 3:28). Most scholars now see “ships passing in the night”—James reacting to a misunderstood Paulinism; Kummel argues chronological distance and ignorance of Pauline polemic after meeting Paul make Jerusalem James impossible. Moo: if written *before* A.D. 48, James lacked direct knowledge of Paul and could attack a perverted “justification by faith alone” slogan from Syrian hearers of early Pauline preaching—fits a middle-40s date.
- **Attribution:** Moo (replying to Kümmel et al.)
- **Quote:** "If, indeed, James 2 fails to come to grips with the real point of Paul's teaching and the letter is written after A.D. 48 or so… then indeed it is difficult to attribute the letter to James of Jerusalem. But suppose the letter was written before A.D. 48."
- **Locus:** Intro § Author, objection 4
- **Tags:** [james-authorship, james-paul-justification, justification, douglas-moo, james-the-just]
- **Type:** position

### C-R0-030
- **Claim:** Moo’s decisive objection to “transparent literary device” pseudepigraphy: little evidence ancient pseudepigraphical epistles were accepted as religiously prescriptive when known to be forged; canonicity of James assumes early Christians thought James wrote it; choice is between forgery (omit from canon) or authentic letter—not “canonical pseudepigraphon.”
- **Attribution:** Moo (citing latest research on forgery reception)
- **Quote:** "No one ever seems to have accepted a document as religiously and philosophically prescriptive which was known to be forged. I do not know of a single example."
- **Locus:** Intro § Author, pseudepigraphy reception objection
- **Tags:** [james-authorship, douglas-moo, james]
- **Type:** position

### C-R0-031
- **Claim:** Compromise views (amanuensis; free translation/redaction of Aramaic/Greek homilies—Davids’s two-stage theory) are possible but, for Moo, unnecessary: Greek is relatively homogeneous (Dibelius); “disjointedness” is genre/purpose; simplest solution is traditional authorship by James of Jerusalem, the Lord’s brother.
- **Attribution:** Moo (engaging Davids, Dibelius)
- **Quote:** "When all the data are considered, the simplest solution is to accept the verdict of early Christians: the letter was written by James of Jerusalem, \"the Lord's brother.\""
- **Locus:** Intro § Author, conclusion
- **Tags:** [james-authorship, douglas-moo, james-the-just]
- **Type:** position

### C-R0-032
- **Claim:** On James’s physical relation to Jesus: Hieronymian (Jerome: *adelphos* = cousin) lacks NT evidence that *adelphos* means cousin; Epiphanian (older son of Joseph by prior wife) vs. Helvidian (born to Joseph and Mary after Jesus); Moo notes NT association of Mary with the brothers may favor Helvidian; Bauckham declines between Epiphanian and Helvidian, slightly inclining Epiphanian.
- **Attribution:** Moo (reporting Jerome/Epiphanius/Helvidius; Bauckham)
- **Quote:** "The close association between Mary and the brothers of Jesus implied in the NT… might favor the Helvidian interpretation."
- **Locus:** Intro § Author, “brother of the Lord” controversy
- **Tags:** [james-the-just, douglas-moo, james-authorship]
- **Type:** position

### C-R0-033
- **Claim:** Readers were almost certainly Jews (scholarly consensus): synagogue (2:2), monotheism (2:19), law centrality, marriage covenant imagery (4:4). “Twelve tribes… diaspora” (1:1) could be spiritualized for the multiethnic church, but Moo prefers a more literal reading given Jewish atmosphere and early date: Jewish Christians living outside Israel.
- **Attribution:** Moo
- **Quote:** "while this interpretation is possible, the Jewish atmosphere of James, along with the probable early date of the letter, makes it more likely that the reference is more literal."
- **Locus:** Intro § Occasion / readers
- **Tags:** [james, douglas-moo]
- **Type:** position

### C-R0-034
- **Claim:** Readers face poverty and oppression (wealthy landowners 5:4–6; rich haul them into court 2:6–7); Moo rejects controlling socioeconomic/liberation or Martin’s anti-Zealot-violence readings: some wealthy believers (1:10; 4:13–17); deeper problem is world *in* the church—“friendship with the world is hatred toward God” (4:4), double-mindedness, and compromise.
- **Attribution:** Moo (vs. liberation theology; Ralph Martin)
- **Quote:** "the letter ultimately has much more to say about the problem of the world getting into the church."
- **Locus:** Intro § Occasion / readers
- **Tags:** [james, douglas-moo, double-mindedness]
- **Type:** position

### C-R0-035
- **Claim:** Date: if Lord’s brother is author, before martyrdom A.D. 62. Moo favors middle 40s, just before Apostolic Council: (1) chap. 2 shows awareness of “justification by faith alone” slogan without grasping authentic Paul—unlikely after A.D. 48/49 Council; perverted Paulinism from hearers of Paul in Tarsus (~36) and Antioch (~45); (2) no awareness of Gentile-mission torah conflict that erupted ~47–48 (Acts 15:1). Judean famine A.D. 46 and rising upheaval fit letter’s situation.
- **Attribution:** Moo
- **Quote:** "we think that James was probably written in the middle 40s, perhaps just before the Apostolic Council."
- **Locus:** Intro § Date
- **Tags:** [james, douglas-moo, james-the-just, james-paul-justification, james-authorship]
- **Type:** position

### C-R0-036
- **Claim:** Charge that James “has no theology” fails: silence on Christology, Spirit, church, OT fulfillment is occasional, not theological emptiness; if theology requires systems built on Christ’s person, James is thin (Jesus named only 1:1; 2:1), but if grounded in God and his purposes, James is thoroughly theological; Johnson: “one of the most ‘theological’ writings in the NT”; no NT document more influenced by Jesus’ teaching.
- **Attribution:** Moo (citing Johnson)
- **Quote:** "No NT document is more influenced by the teaching of Jesus than James."
- **Locus:** Intro § Theology (opening)
- **Tags:** [james, douglas-moo]
- **Type:** position

### C-R0-037
- **Claim:** Three characteristics of God are especially important in James: oneness, jealousy, and grace. Oneness: monotheist confession (2:19; 4:11); God as “single” in giving (1:5) and constant (1:17) contrasts human *dipsychos* dividedness (1:8; 4:4, 8); all commandments must be obeyed (2:11).
- **Attribution:** Moo
- **Quote:** "Three characteristics of God are especially important in James: his oneness, his jealousy, and his grace."
- **Locus:** Intro § Theology — God
- **Tags:** [james, douglas-moo, double-mindedness]
- **Type:** position

### C-R0-038
- **Claim:** Despite undeveloped christology, “Lord” applies to God and Jesus; one Judge (4:11) yet Jesus as eschatological judge (5:7, 9) yields “incipient trinitarianism” without modifying monotheism. God’s jealousy (4:5, contested translation) substantiates call to abandon world-friendship; same context, God “gives us more grace” (4:6).
- **Attribution:** Moo
- **Quote:** "We find in the juxtaposition of these points an incipient trinitarianism."
- **Locus:** Intro § Theology — God
- **Tags:** [james, douglas-moo]
- **Type:** position

### C-R0-039
- **Claim:** Future eschatology dominates (judgment warnings; rewards; “Lord’s coming is near,” Judge at the door 5:8–9); “nearness” means next event on the divine timetable and possibility at any time, not certainty within a few years. Present inaugurated eschatology also present (kingdom inheritance 2:5 with royal law 2:8; new birth 1:18; wealth hoarded “in the last days” 5:3)—“fulfillment without consummation.”
- **Attribution:** Moo
- **Quote:** "James… motivates his readers to godly living not by insisting that the Lord would come at any moment but by reminding them that he could."
- **Locus:** Intro § Theology — Eschatology
- **Tags:** [james, douglas-moo]
- **Type:** position

### C-R0-040
- **Claim:** Law appears in ethical exhortations: perfect law of liberty (1:25; 2:12), royal law/love command (2:8), unity of law (2:10–11), slander as criticism of the law (4:11). Little ritual concern is occasional focus, not proof against Jerusalem James. Leviticus 19 clusters (love, swearing, wages, partiality, slander) are basic for Johnson and Moo.
- **Attribution:** Moo (engaging Johnson on Lev 19)
- **Quote:** "James read at least this section of Leviticus 19 as a summary of the basic intent of the law."
- **Locus:** Intro § Theology — Law
- **Tags:** [james, douglas-moo]
- **Type:** position

### C-R0-041
- **Claim:** Qualifiers “royal,” “perfect,” “of liberty” carry Christian nuance: *basilikos* linked to *basileia* (2:5)—love command royal as from Jesus the King / chief law of the kingdom; “perfect law of liberty” replaces “word” (1:22–23), the planted “word of truth” of new birth (1:18, 21), alluding to Jer. 31:31–34 internalized law. Law not simply replaced by Jesus’ teaching alone (OT allusions remain); Christians cannot take gospel benefits without obeying God’s word as law.
- **Attribution:** Moo
- **Quote:** "James's description of the law as \"planted in\" the believer almost certainly alludes to the famous \"new covenant\" prophecy of Jer. 31:31-34."
- **Locus:** Intro § Theology — Law
- **Tags:** [james, douglas-moo]
- **Type:** position

### C-R0-042
- **Claim:** On alleged Paul–James contradiction over law (Luther: James’s “law of liberty” vs. Paul’s law of slavery/wrath/death): Paul’s salvation-historical “not under law” is largely negative yet he also relates Christians to OT law in places; Moo prefers that James maintains OT law’s authority only as “fulfilled” by Jesus—Wessel: “law of freedom” as Palestinian Jew’s description of Christian *didache*—yoke easy/burden light (Matt. 11:30).
- **Attribution:** Moo (citing Wessel; Cadoux on tension severity)
- **Quote:** "'law of freedom' is a Palestinian Jew's way of describing the Christian standard of conduct found in the didache."
- **Locus:** Intro § Theology — Law (vs. Paul)
- **Tags:** [james, douglas-moo, james-paul-justification]
- **Type:** position

### C-R0-043
- **Claim:** Wisdom (1:5 for trials/maturity; 3:13–18 earthly vs. heavenly, fruit-like list) is OT-style (Proverbs/Sirach), without intertestamental personified/semidivine wisdom or torah-identification developments used elsewhere in NT christology. Davids: wisdom in James functions as Spirit does in Paul (fruit parallel to Gal. 5:22–23)—Moo allows only for that narrow point; wisdom is not the letter’s central integrating concept.
- **Attribution:** Moo (engaging Davids)
- **Quote:** "while wisdom certainly has its place in James's theology, it cannot be given the central and integrating role that some scholars have wanted to give it."
- **Locus:** Intro § Theology — Wisdom
- **Tags:** [james, douglas-moo, wisdom-literature]
- **Type:** position

### C-R0-044
- **Claim:** Poverty/wealth tradition (Mussner): God chooses the poor (2:5 // Ps/Deut; care of orphans/widows 1:27); OT “poor”/righteous and “rich”/wicked association via Jesus’ beatitudes/woes (Luke 6:20, 24) fuels liberation readings. Moo rejects simple identity: 1:10–11 likely a rich Christian brother; 5:1–6 condemns specific sins (hoarding, luxury, defrauding, persecution). Still, possessing wealth while others lack necessities can be sinful—a word Western churches need; avoid both radicalizing and trivializing.
- **Attribution:** Moo
- **Quote:** "The very possession of wealth, when others are going without the basic necessities of life, suggests James, is sinful"
- **Locus:** Intro § Theology — Poverty and Wealth
- **Tags:** [james, douglas-moo]
- **Type:** position

### C-R0-045
- **Claim:** Ethics is James’s most important NT theological contribution, set in inaugurated-eschatology: born again (1:18) but not yet saved (1:21; 2:14; 5:20); goal “perfect and complete” (1:4); essence of the problem is *dipsychos* “double-mindedness” (waves 1:6; blessing/cursing 3:9–10; profession without practice 2:14–26). Moo quotes Wesley on Christian perfection as purity of intention / giving God all the heart.
- **Attribution:** Moo (quoting Wesley)
- **Quote:** "Human \"dividedness,\" the condition James calls dipsychos, \"double-minded\" or \"double-souled,\" is the essence of the problem."
- **Locus:** Intro § Theology — Christian life
- **Tags:** [james, douglas-moo, double-mindedness]
- **Type:** definition

### C-R0-046
- **Claim:** Prayer emphasis: God gives good gifts (1:17) and answers (1:5); condition is faith (1:6–8; 5:14), not selfish asking (4:3); Elijah as righteous yet frail model (5:17–18).
- **Attribution:** Moo
- **Quote:** "James is especially concerned that we understand the condition for receiving our requests from God: faith (1:6-8; 5:14)."
- **Locus:** Intro § Theology — Christian life (prayer)
- **Tags:** [james, douglas-moo]
- **Type:** position

### C-R0-047
- **Claim:** On faith/works (2:14–26): James condemns sterile, actionless orthodoxy; faith establishes relationship with God but genuine faith always produces righteous living; “faith without deeds is dead/useless.” Sterile verbal profession (2:19) is not James’s own view of faith—faith is firm commitment (2:1), refined in trials, grasping promises in prayer. On faith’s meaning James and Paul agree (Gal. 5:6 “faith working through love”).
- **Attribution:** Moo
- **Quote:** "Genuine faith, he insists, always and inevitably produces evidence of its existence in a life of righteous living."
- **Locus:** Intro § Theology — Faith, Works, and Justification
- **Tags:** [james, douglas-moo, justification, james-paul-justification]
- **Type:** position

### C-R0-048
- **Claim:** Apparent contradiction remains on works’ place: Paul “justified by faith apart from works of the law” (Rom. 3:28) vs. James “justified by works and not by faith alone” (2:24). “Works of the law” vs. “works” distinction cannot ground harmonization—they mean the same thing at bottom (details deferred to exegesis of 2:21–26).
- **Attribution:** Moo
- **Quote:** "at bottom, they mean the same thing; and so harmonization of the two perspectives cannot be based on this distinction."
- **Locus:** Intro § Theology — Faith/Works/Justification
- **Tags:** [james-paul-justification, justification, douglas-moo, james]
- **Type:** position

### C-R0-049
- **Claim:** Second-temple Jewish soteriology is usefully framed as “covenantal nomism” (grace of covenant; law as response to “stay in,” not “get in”), but Moo qualifies: diversity within Judaism includes more legalistic groups; and belonging to the covenant was not automatic final salvation—judgment required personal commitment to obey; second-temple soteriology was synergistic.
- **Attribution:** Moo (engaging covenantal nomism paradigm)
- **Quote:** "second-temple Jewish soteriology was synergistic: it required human beings to cooperate with God's grace through obedience to the law for salvation."
- **Locus:** Intro § Theology — Faith/Works (covenantal nomism)
- **Tags:** [covenantal-nomism, douglas-moo, justification, james]
- **Type:** position

### C-R0-050
- **Claim:** Surface pattern of James 2 seems to match new-covenant covenantal nomism: birth by grace through word of truth (1:18); faith foundation (2:1; Abraham 2:22–23); final salvation/justification takes works into account—get in by faith, stay in by obedience to royal law. Many rest there; Moo insists canonical integration with Paul is necessary if NT is one revelation.
- **Attribution:** Moo
- **Quote:** "one \"gets into\" relationship with God by faith in Christ, but \"stays in\" that relationship through obedience to the \"royal law\" (2:8)."
- **Locus:** Intro § Theology — Faith/Works (James & nomism)
- **Tags:** [covenantal-nomism, justification, james-paul-justification, douglas-moo, james]
- **Type:** position

### C-R0-051
- **Claim:** Two integration alternatives: find synergism in Paul too (often two “justifications”: initial by faith, final by works+faith—common in some Catholic and Protestant theologians), or monergism in both. Moo rejects synergistic Paul: justification by faith means entry by faith alone *and* a final verdict guaranteeing ultimate salvation; works are God’s work/Spirit fruit (Phil. 2:13)—not synergism.
- **Attribution:** Moo
- **Quote:** "Paul, in other words, teaches a monergistic view of salvation: God himself provides it."
- **Locus:** Intro § Theology — Faith/Works (integration)
- **Tags:** [justification, james-paul-justification, douglas-moo]
- **Type:** position

### C-R0-052
- **Claim:** Popular evangelical reading of James “justify” as mere demonstration of righteousness (removing soteriology) cannot be sustained—justification in James 2 is God’s ultimate vindication in judgment. Better theologically: use “justification” for Paul’s teaching and “judgment” for James 2. Harmonization: read James’s “works” via Pauline Spirit-produced works; true faith “works” rather than works being “added”; Laato links monergism to creative power of new birth (1:18).
- **Attribution:** Moo (citing T. Laato)
- **Quote:** "What appears on the surface to be synergism in James can, without contradiction with anything James says, be read in light of the monergism of Paul."
- **Locus:** Intro § Theology — Faith/Works (monergistic sketch)
- **Tags:** [justification, james-paul-justification, douglas-moo, james]
- **Type:** position

### C-R0-053
- **Claim:** Pastoral contrast: Paul strikes at legalism (Judaizers); James at quietism (professors dismissing obedience). Luther faced works-heavy medieval Catholicism (Paul-focus); Wesley faced moral indifference (James-focus). James does not require 100% conformity (3:2) but total unconcern for obedience must put claimed saving faith in question.
- **Attribution:** Moo
- **Quote:** "Paul strikes at legalism; James at quietism. Each message needs to be heard."
- **Locus:** Intro § Theology — Faith/Works (closing pastoral)
- **Tags:** [james-paul-justification, justification, douglas-moo, james]
- **Type:** position

### C-R0-054
- **Claim:** Structure debate: Luther/Dibelius saw chaotic/loose paraenesis; recent scholarship finds more unity—Adamson “sustained unity”; Davids (after F. O. Francis): double opening 1:2–27, body 2:1–5:6, conclusion 5:7–20, with repeated themes testing, wisdom/speech, poverty/wealth; Frankemölle: 1:2–18 exordium / 5:7–20 peroratio framing body with themes announced in opening.
- **Attribution:** Moo (surveying Adamson, Davids, Francis, Frankemölle)
- **Quote:** "the last three decades have witnessed a serious reconsideration of this matter of James's structure."
- **Locus:** Intro § Structure and Theme
- **Tags:** [james, douglas-moo]
- **Type:** structure

### C-R0-055
- **Claim:** Moo’s own structural proposal: more organization than Dibelius, less than Frankemölle. Persistent motifs: testing (1:2–4, 12; 5:7–11) as *context* not sole topic; poverty/oppression (1:9–11; 2:1–13; 5:1–6); not Davids’s clear third theme wisdom/speech (other topics equal). Body 1:2–5:11 in five sections: (1) 1:2–18 trials-unifying; (2) 1:19–2:26 obedience to the word; (3) 3:1–4:12 speech + envy/violence topos, with 4:4–10 climax standing apart; (4) 4:13–5:11 arrogance/rich/patience; (5 left implicit with closing materials).
- **Attribution:** Moo
- **Quote:** "we think the body of the letter (1:2-5:11) can be divided into five general sections."
- **Locus:** Intro § Structure and Theme
- **Tags:** [james, douglas-moo]
- **Type:** structure

### C-R0-056
- **Claim:** Central concern (better than narrow “theme”): spiritual wholeness, discovered at emotional climax 4:4–10—readers castigated as “adulteresses” (covenant marriage imagery); friendship with the world makes God enemy; *dipsychos* double-mindedness (1:8; 4:8); stark oppositions (loyalty vs. compromise, wisdom from above vs. worldly, pure religion vs. self-deception). Readers must stop compromising with worldly values and give themselves wholly to the Lord.
- **Attribution:** Moo
- **Quote:** "Spiritual \"wholeness,\" then, we suggest, is the central concern of the letter."
- **Locus:** Intro § Structure and Theme (closing)
- **Tags:** [james, douglas-moo, double-mindedness]
- **Type:** position

### C-R0-057
- **Claim:** Anointing/healing of James 5 is not developed as a discrete introductory controversy in this range; elders as spiritual leaders appear only as a datum of “primitive Christian theology” (5:14) within the authorship corroboration sketch.
- **Attribution:** Moo (incidental mention only)
- **Quote:** "\"elders\" functioning as spiritual leaders in the local church (5:14)."
- **Locus:** Intro § Author (primitive theology list)
- **Tags:** [anointing-healing-james-5, james, douglas-moo]
- **Type:** fact

### C-R0-058
- **Claim:** Moo’s pastoral self-application in the preface: churches filled with halfhearted believers leaving large life-areas untouched by Christian values; his own midlife “tendency to back off” in fervor was challenged by reimmersion in James.
- **Attribution:** Moo
- **Quote:** "Our churches are filled with believers who are only halfhearted in their faith and, as a result, leave large areas of their lives virtually untouched by genuine Christian values."
- **Locus:** Author’s preface
- **Tags:** [douglas-moo, james, moo-james-pntc]
- **Type:** reception
